opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's actually something I've been noticing quite a bit in my own day-to-day work. When the reasoning models first came out, there was this tendency to just crank everything up to the highest effort setting, because you assumed more thinking meant better answers. And for really hard problems, like debugging something subtle in a training loop or working through a tricky derivation, that's often still true. But it comes at a cost. You wait a long time, and it burns a lot of tokens, and honestly, for many of my everyday tasks it's overkill.

What's changed is that the lower and medium reasoning-effort settings have gotten surprisingly good. So now I find myself using the model more like an interactive collaborator again, rather than something I hand a task to and then go get coffee while it thinks. If I want to quickly refactor a function, write a small test, check whether I'm using a PyTorch API correctly, or get feedback on a paragraph in a book chapter, the low-effort mode is fast enough that it stays in the flow of what I'm doing. That matters a lot, because once you have to context-switch, the productivity benefit kind of evaporates.

So my workflow has become a bit more tiered, I'd say. I default to the lower setting for the quick, iterative stuff, and I consciously escalate to high reasoning only when I hit something where I can tell the model needs to actually work through multiple steps. It's a bit like how you wouldn't schedule a long meeting with a senior colleague for a question you could resolve in a quick chat.

And I think from a research perspective, that's also interesting, because it suggests the models are getting more efficient at reasoning itself. It's not just "think longer to get better." The training, whether that's better reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards or distillation from the stronger reasoning traces, seems to be making the shorter reasoning paths more effective. That has big practical implications too, especially for cost and latency, and for running things locally. If you can get most of the benefit with a fraction of the tokens, that makes these models much more usable in real applications, not just in benchmark settings.

That said, I still try to stay in the loop. Even when the fast mode gives me something that looks right, I read it, I run it, I check it. Lower effort makes it easier to iterate quickly, but it doesn't replace understanding what's going on. For me, it's really about using the model to speed up the parts that are tedious, so I can spend more of my own thinking on the parts that are actually interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says lower and medium effort work well for many everyday tasks, defaults to lower effort for iterative work, and escalates to high effort only for harder, multi-step problems.

r002.rationale: It links faster results to staying in the flow and using the model interactively, but does not describe a shift from occasional use to routine workflow integration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and it's actually something I've been paying attention to a lot lately. So for a while, the story was basically: if you want good answers, you crank up the reasoning effort, you let the model think for a long time, you pay for all those tokens, and you wait. And for certain things, like a tricky math problem or a subtle bug, that's still worth it. But what I've noticed over the past year or so is that the low and medium settings have gotten dramatically better. The gap between "think a little" and "think a lot" has narrowed for a huge fraction of everyday tasks.

And that changes how I use these models, because latency really matters for the kind of work I do. When I'm writing code or writing a chapter for a book, I'm in a flow state, and if I have to wait thirty seconds for a response, I'll just not ask. I'll figure it out myself. But if the model comes back in two or three seconds with something that's right ninety-plus percent of the time, then it becomes more like a conversation partner, or almost like a really fast pair programmer sitting next to you. So the LLM moves from being this tool I consult occasionally for hard problems to something that's woven into every step.

The other thing is cost, especially for people like me who run a lot of experiments. I do a lot of educational content, implementing things from scratch, and I often use LLMs to help generate test cases, check my understanding, or summarize a paper quickly. If I can do that at low effort and get a reliable answer, I can do it hundreds of times a day without thinking about it. That's a very different workflow from carefully rationing your high-effort calls.

I would also say there's a kind of division of labor emerging. I now think of the low-effort setting as the default, and I escalate deliberately. If something looks off, or it's a genuinely hard problem, that's when I bump the effort up. It's a bit like how you'd work with a colleague, honestly. You don't ask them to go away and write a ten-page analysis for every little question. You ask quickly, and only when it's a hard question do you say, "take your time on this one."

And from a research perspective, I find it fascinating, because it tells us something about where the capability actually lives. A lot of what used to require long chains of thought is now, in some sense, being distilled into the base model's immediate responses. The reasoning traces from the high-effort runs become training data, and the model internalizes patterns that it used to have to work out explicitly. So the improvement at low effort is really a signal of the whole system getting better, not just a cheaper mode.

r001.rationale: The response says low and medium settings now work reliably for a huge fraction of everyday tasks, with low effort as the default and escalation reserved for hard problems. This communicates that most tasks do not need extra-high effort.

r002.rationale: It links faster responses to using the model throughout coding and writing, shifting from occasional consultation to a tool woven into every step.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes LLMs more useful for the everyday tasks where you don’t want to wait for a long reasoning process. In a coding workflow, for example, you might have a small question, want to understand a function, or make a quick change. If a lower reasoning-effort setting can handle that reliably, you get a much faster feedback loop.

Then I can reserve the higher reasoning settings for problems that actually need them—debugging something subtle, or thinking through a more complicated implementation. The important thing for me is whether the answer is useful and how much checking it requires. If the faster setting gives me a good starting point with less back-and-forth, that’s a meaningful improvement. It makes the model easier to use throughout the work, while I’m still making the decisions and checking the results.

r001.rationale: The response reserves higher reasoning settings for subtle or complex problems, but it does not say medium-high effort is sufficient for most tasks.

r002.rationale: It connects faster feedback to easier use throughout the work, but does not clearly describe a shift from occasional LLM use to routine workflow integration.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it makes LLMs more useful for the small, everyday tasks where waiting for a long answer would interrupt what I’m doing. If I’m asking about a piece of code or working through an idea, I want a quick response that helps me take the next step. If the lower reasoning-effort setting gets better, I can use it for more of those interactions and reserve the higher setting for problems that actually need it.

I still have to check the result, especially with research or code. But the balance shifts: instead of deciding whether a question is worth handing off to the model, I can bring it into the workflow more routinely. The interesting part is whether it saves time overall, including the time I spend reviewing and correcting the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says to reserve a higher setting for problems that need it, but does not say medium-high effort is sufficient for most tasks or mention extra-high effort.

r002.rationale: It connects quicker results and less disruptive waiting with using LLMs more routinely in the workflow.
